did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm’s title attributes it to the Sons of Korah and indicates that it is intended for the music director; the Sons of Korah are mentioned in the titles of several Psalms.
Did you know? The psalm addresses “all peoples,” not only Israel, and calls them to clap their hands and shout to God with joyful voices.
Did you know? The LORD is described here as “a great King over all the earth,” emphasizing his kingship and universal rule.
Did you know? According to the wording of the psalm, the LORD’s rule also involves subduing peoples and nations: “He subdues peoples under us and nations under our feet.”
Did you know? The psalm calls Israel’s inheritance “the pride of Jacob” and presents it as an inheritance that the LORD chose and loved.
Did you know? The divine ascent is described with the sound of a joyful shout and a trumpet blast—two sounds associated in the text with celebration, proclamation, and joy.
Did you know? In this verse, the call to “sing” is repeated four times, emphasizing the central role of singing in praising God and the King.
Did you know? The word “maskil” at the end of the verse appears as part of the psalm’s musical or literary instruction, alongside the call to sing to God.
Did you know? The psalm presents God as reigning over the nations and sitting on “his holy throne,” combining universal kingship with holiness.

Did you know? At the end of the psalm, the nobles of the peoples gather with “the people of the God of Abraham,” and the verse concludes by declaring that “the shields of the earth” belong to God and that he is highly exalted.
